sentences: Beneath snow-covered mountains, plum trees have burst into flowers as white as snowflakes.
Hidden among them is a small thatched house.
This is Plum Blossoms and a Thatched House, painted by Jeon Gi, who signed himself Goram, in the late Joseon period.
It is painted in light colour on paper, a small picture only a little more than thirty centimetres on each side.
It belongs to the National Museum of Korea, part of the Dongwon collection given by the collector Lee Hong-kun.
Look first at the thatched house in the middle of the picture.
Inside, a figure dressed in green sits quietly by the window.
The museum suggests that this is probably Oh Gyeong-seok, the friend who received the painting as a gift.
Now look at the plum trees.
Their trunks and branches are drawn in dark, continuous lines of ink, and every flower is a single dot of white pigment.
That is why the blossoms seem to swirl around the house like snowflakes in the wind.
Look too at the white mountains and the heavy, frowning sky behind them.
Pale ink is layered softly to give the slopes their light and shade, and blue-green moss dots are set upright on top of them.
These bold blue-green dots are regarded as a hallmark of the coloured plum paintings of this period.
Near the bottom of the picture there is a short inscription.
It tells us that the painting was made for Oh Gyeong-seok, whose pen name was Yeongmae.
Oh was a government interpreter who travelled back and forth to China, and he later became an important figure among Korea's reformers.
Pictures like this are known as plum-blossom studio paintings.
The Song-dynasty poet Lin Bu is said to have lived alone on a remote hill by the West Lake, loving only his plum trees and his cranes.
Late Joseon painters borrowed his story and loved to paint a scholar sitting in a study wrapped in blossom.
Jeon Gi was born in 1825 and died in 1854.
He belonged to the jungin, the middle class of technical specialists, and ran a business in medicinal herbs.
He also collected and judged old calligraphy and paintings, and dealt in them.
He studied with the great scholar Kim Jeong-hui, known as Chusa, and was a member of Byeogosa, a poetry society of middle-class writers and artists.
In the summer of 1849, a contest was held at his own house in which Kim Jeong-hui judged the calligraphy and paintings of his pupils.
The master's comments were gathered into a book called Yerim gabeullok.
Because Jeon Gi died before he reached the age of thirty, only a small number of his works survive.
Step back and look at it again: snowy mountains, plum trees in white bloom, and a friend's house waiting for a visitor among them, a small picture made in friendship.
This winter, think of someone you would like to send a little news of plum blossom to.
